context: Dante is still on the far bank from Beatrice. She speaks to him across the water, and he may not cross until he has confessed.

note: The sword she promised in Canto 30. Until now she has spoken about Dante to the angels, and that was the edge of the blade. Now she turns and speaks straight at him: the point.
In the sacrament of penance, sorrow is not enough: the sinner must say the sin aloud. Beatrice has laid out the charge, and Dante must own it in his own voice.
Lethe wipes out the memory of sin, but Dante has not drunk from it yet. He cannot plead that he has forgotten.

quote: you'd need eyes to understand the sound
note: His "Yes" is so faint that it could be read on his lips but not heard.
God. Loving Beatrice was meant to lead Dante on to the love of God, the one good that leaves nothing more to want.
The whole of Dante's confession, three lines long. "Present things", in his Italian: the goods of this world, close at hand, which took her place once she was dead. He names nothing more exact.
God, who knows every sin whether it is confessed or not.

quote: the grinding wheel turns back against the blade
note: A whetstone turned against the edge blunts a blade instead of sharpening it. In Heaven's court, a sinner's own confession blunts the sword of justice.

context: Beatrice's name for the false pleasures that drew Dante away. He dreamed of a Siren in Canto 19, a hag who turned beautiful as he stared at her.

note: Her argument: her body was the most beautiful thing Dante had ever seen, and it died. That should have taught him that no mortal thing can be trusted to last, and sent him after what cannot die.
No longer a mortal, deceiving thing. As a soul in Heaven she had become a lasting good, and more worth following than before.

The Italian word is "pargoletta", a young girl. Dante wrote love poems to a woman he calls by that word, and no one knows who she was. Some readers take Beatrice to mean a real rival, others a figure for any passing attraction.
An echo of Proverbs 1:17: "in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird". A fledgling may be fooled two or three times. Dante was a grown man, and should have learned from the first wound.
Dante's Italian says "lift up your beard". That one word is the insult he feels a few lines later.
"Our wind", in the Italian: the north wind that blows down over Italy from Europe.
Dante says "the land of Iarbas", the African king who courted Dido in the Aeneid. The wind from there is the south wind.
She said "beard" where she could have said "face". The sting is that he is a bearded man, not the fledgling of her comparison, and has no excuse of youth.
The angels on the chariot, who have been scattering flowers since Beatrice appeared.

context: "One person in two natures" is the language the Church uses of Christ, who is both God and man. It is the plainest sign in the poem of what the griffin stands for.

note: Even veiled and across the river, she is more beautiful now than she was on earth, and on earth she was more beautiful than any other woman. It is the answer to her charge that he loved her less after she died.
Dante's word is a nettle. This is the sorrow for sin that penance requires: he now hates whatever drew him away from her.
Dante faints, as he did on the shore of Acheron (Inferno 3) and after hearing Francesca (Inferno 5). Those were faints of terror and pity. This one comes from knowing his own guilt.

quote: the lady I had found alone
context: Dante met her in Canto 28, singing and picking flowers on the far bank of Lethe. She has not yet been named.

note: She skims over the surface while Dante is pulled through the water up to his neck. The Italian word may mean a weaver's shuttle or a light, quick boat.

"Asperges me", from Psalm 51 (50 in the Latin Bible), the great psalm of repentance: "You will sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be clean; you will wash me and I shall be whiter than snow." It is sung in church when the priest sprinkles the people with holy water.
Drinking from Lethe takes away the memory of his sins. The plunge under water also looks like a baptism.

context: The four ladies in purple who danced at the chariot's left wheel in Canto 29. Now that Dante is cleansed, they take him into their dance.

note: The four stars Dante saw over the southern pole when he came out of Hell, shining on Cato's face (Purgatorio 1).

quote: Before Beatrice descended to the world
note: Before she was born. The virtues were chosen to serve her from the beginning, which makes her life part of God's plan and not a private love story.

context: The three ladies at the chariot's right wheel. The four cardinal virtues can bring Dante as far as Beatrice's eyes. It takes faith, hope and love, which see deeper, to make him able to look into them.

note: Beatrice's eyes. Whether Dante means that they were green is uncertain: emeralds were prized for their brightness, and green is the color of hope.
The language of the love poetry of Dante's youth, where the god of Love shoots his arrows from the lady's eyes.

quote: sometimes showing one nature, sometimes the other
note: The griffin itself does not change, but its reflection in her eyes shows now the eagle, now the lion. Usually read as the way the human mind grasps Christ: as God at one moment, as man at the next, never both at once. Seeing the two together is kept for the last lines of Paradiso.
An echo of what Wisdom says of herself in the Bible: "Those who eat of me will hunger for more" (Sirach 24).
Faith, hope and love. They rank above the four cardinal virtues, and it is they who ask Beatrice to unveil.
A generous name for the man she has just convicted of unfaithfulness. With the confession made and Lethe crossed, the charge is behind him.
Her mouth, and its smile. The first beauty was her eyes. Dante wrote elsewhere that a lady's eyes and smile are the two places where the soul shows itself.

quote: O splendor of eternal living light
note: Addressed to Beatrice's unveiled face, which reflects the light of God. Dante does not try to describe it. He says only that no poet could.

Parnassus is the mountain in Greece sacred to Apollo and the Muses, and its spring, Castalia, was said to give poets their gift. To grow pale in its shadow is to wear oneself out studying the art of poetry.
